summary: Most visitors to Suriname need no visa but must pay an Entry Fee online before travel — USD or EUR 50 for a single entry or 75 for multiple entries, plus a service fee, for stays of up to 90 days. CARICOM nationals are exempt, and 21 nationalities, including India, South Africa and Nigeria, need an eVisa.

passportValidity.text: Your passport must be valid for at least 6 months from the date you leave Suriname, and have at least one blank page for the immigration stamp. If it has less than 6 months left, renew it before applying for an eVisa.

conflict.states: 6 months after the date you arrive

source.name: Suriname eVisa and Entry Fee service — FAQs

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever certificate is required from travelers aged 1 year and over arriving from a country with risk of transmission, including those who transited for more than 12 hours through an airport in such a country. Suriname is itself a country with risk of yellow fever transmission, and Guyana asks for the certificate from travelers arriving from it.

source.name: WHO, International Travel and Health, Annex 1 — countries requiring proof of vaccination against yellow fever
source.instrument: International Health Regulations (2005), Article 36 and Annex 7; WHO International Travel and Health, Annex 1, 18 November 2022 (revised 3 January 2023)

vaccinations.name: Malaria prophylaxis
vaccinations.text: Not an entry requirement. Paramaribo and the coastal strip are essentially malaria-free, but the interior and the gold-mining districts are not. Take advice from a travel clinic if you are going upriver.

source.name: WHO — International Travel and Health country list: vaccination requirements (Suriname)

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not checked at the border, but hospital care in Paramaribo must be paid for and anything serious means evacuation to Trinidad, the Netherlands or the United States — cover including medical evacuation is strongly recommended, especially for jungle trips.

source.name: Government of Suriname — entry requirements

onwardTicket.text: Entry Fee and visa holders should hold a confirmed return or onward ticket within the permitted stay; airlines check this before boarding for Johan Adolf Pengel International Airport.

source.name: Government of Suriname — entry requirements

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published, though officers may ask about your accommodation and means of support. Visa applications normally include bank statements for the period of the trip.

source.name: Government of Suriname — visa information

declarations.name: Entry Fee voucher or eVisa
declarations.text: The Entry Fee voucher or eVisa is emailed to you as a PDF; there is no passport stamping before travel. Keep a copy — printed as well as on your phone — to show at check-in and at immigration in Paramaribo.

source.name: Suriname eVisa and Entry Fee service — FAQs

declarations.name: Immigration and Customs Form (ICF)
declarations.submitWindow: Up to 3 days before arrival, and again before departure
declarations.text: All travellers to and from Suriname must complete an Immigration and Customs Form (ICF) up to three days before arrival and up to three days before departure.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Suriname entry requirements

currencyLimits.text: Cash or negotiable instruments worth EUR 10,000 or more, or the equivalent in another currency, must be declared to customs on arrival and departure.

source.name: Government of Suriname — customs

notes: Gold cannot simply be carried out of the country — exports are controlled and require documentation.
Wildlife products, including caiman and jaguar items and untreated feathers, are prohibited under CITES rules.
Fresh food, plants and seeds are restricted; declare anything agricultural rather than risk a penalty.

payments.text: Cards are accepted in Paramaribo's larger hotels, supermarkets and a few restaurants, but foreign cards are often declined and ATMs do not always accept them. Bring US dollars or euros in cash to change at a bank or licensed cambio, and carry Surinamese dollars for the interior, where there is no banking at all.

safety.text: Burglary, armed robbery and violent crime occur in Paramaribo and the surrounding areas; criminals may target people in quiet or secluded places, including the Palm Garden (Palmentuin), and pickpocketing and robbery are increasingly common in the main business and shopping areas. Tourists have been robbed when travelling in central Suriname, away from the coast, so use a well-established tour company there.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Suriname travel advice (safety and security)

bestTimeToVisit.text: Suriname has two dry seasons — a short one in February and March and a long one from August to November. The long dry season is best for river trips, jungle lodges and the sea-turtle beaches at Galibi.

tips.text: Pay the Entry Fee (or get your eVisa) before you leave home, and only through the government's official service at suriname.vfsevisa.com, linked from gov.sr. The search results are full of look-alike commercial sites charging more than the real price.

Dutch is the official language and the one used on signs and paperwork, with Sranan Tongo as the everyday lingua franca. English is widely understood in Paramaribo's tourism trade but much less so in the interior.

Carry cash. The Surinamese dollar has been through heavy devaluations, foreign cards are often refused, and prices for tours are frequently quoted in US dollars or euros. Bring clean, undamaged notes to change at a bank or cambio.

The rainforest interior — Bigi Pan, the Upper Suriname river villages, Raleighvallen — is reached by shared taxi and dugout canoe or by a small plane, and effectively has to be booked as a package. Allow a spare day either side of an international flight.

Suriname drives on the left, a legacy it shares with neighboring Guyana, and the road east into French Guiana ends at a ferry across the Marowijne river. If you plan to drive on, check the ferry timetable and the French border requirements in advance.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Suriname?
faq.answer: Most visitors do not need a visa but must pay Suriname's Entry Fee online before travel: USD or EUR 50 for a single entry, or 75 for up to five entries within three months, plus an 8 service fee, for stays of up to 90 days. That covers citizens of the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, the EU, Australia and most other countries. CARICOM nationals are exempt. Since May 2023, 21 nationalities — including India, South Africa, Nigeria, Pakistan and Bangladesh — need an eVisa instead.

faq.question: What is the difference between the Entry Fee and a Surinamese visa?
faq.answer: Since 1 July 2022, visitors coming for tourism pay the Entry Fee instead of getting a visa. It is paid online, needs no invitation letter, and covers tourism and family visits of up to 90 days — one entry, or up to five within three months. A visa is needed for business trips, for leaving the airport while in transit, and by the 21 nationalities that are not eligible for the Entry Fee.

faq.question: Can I pay the Suriname Entry Fee on arrival?
faq.answer: Plan to pay it before you travel. The Entry Fee is paid online through the official service and the voucher is emailed to you as a PDF; keep a copy to show at check-in and on arrival.

faq.question: Do CARICOM citizens pay the Suriname Entry Fee?
faq.answer: No. Holders of passports from CARICOM countries are exempt from the Entry Fee and listed as visa-exempt. Haiti is the exception in practice: Suriname's eVisa service states that direct flights from Haiti are not allowed and that it will not issue visas to Haitian citizens.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever certificate for Suriname?
faq.answer: It is required from age 1 if you are arriving from — or have transited — a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. Suriname is itself a risk country, so vaccination is recommended for everyone, and the certificate is checked when you travel on to Brazil, Guyana or French Guiana.

faq.question: Can I extend my stay in Suriname?
faq.answer: Yes, in principle. Apply to the immigration authorities in Paramaribo before your permitted stay runs out; extensions are usually granted in short blocks and require your accommodation details and onward ticket. It is simpler to plan the trip within the 90 days allowed on entry than to extend later.
